# Tools and code

This page describes how a workflow calls HTTP APIs and runs Python. Read [workflow-format.md](workflow-format.md) first.

Statements marked "verified in a working builder" come from a builder that created a 6-node workflow through the REST API. The workflow has code nodes, `api_call` tools, post-hooks and transitions on tool results. Its agent passed its practice cases. Statements marked "seen in a trial call" come from the event log of a simulation call made with that builder.

## Tool function shape

Every external action is a **tool function**. The shape is the same wherever you attach it.

```json
{
  "type": "function",
  "config": { "timeoutMs": 10000, "maxRetries": 2 },
  "function": {
    "name": "lookup_order",
    "handler": "__function__:api_call",
    "description": "Look up one order. CALL it when the caller asks about a specific order.",
    "parameters": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "url": { "type": "string", "default": "https://api.example.com/v1/orders/lookup" },
        "method": { "type": "string", "default": "POST" },
        "headers": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": { "Content-Type": { "type": "string", "default": "application/json" } }
        },
        "body": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": {
            "customer_id": { "type": "string", "default": "{{customer_id}}" },
            "order_number": { "type": "string", "description": "Order number, digits only", "default": "{{order_number}}" }
          },
          "required": ["order_number"]
        }
      }
    }
  },
  "response_mapping": [
    { "path": "data.status", "variable": "order_status" }
  ]
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `type` | Always `"function"` |
| `function.name` | Tool name. The model calls it by this name. Result variables are named after it |
| `function.handler` | Which runtime executes the tool. See the table below |
| `function.description` | Read by the dialogue model when the tool is in `tools`. Ignored in `pre_actions` |
| `function.parameters` | JSON-schema object. `properties` holds the parameters |
| `config.timeoutMs` | Timeout of one attempt, in milliseconds |
| `config.maxRetries` | Tool-level retries of a failed call |
| `config.interruptible` | `false` makes the tool run in the background. See "Background tools" |
| `config.alwaysRunsAt` | Makes the tool a lifecycle tool. See "Lifecycle tools" |
| `response_mapping` | Tool level, for tools in `tools`. Maps the result to variables |
| `pre_process_code` | Python hook that runs before the call |
| `post_process_code` | Python hook that runs after the call |

| Handler | Runs |
|---|---|
| `__function__:api_call` | An HTTP request |
| `__function__:code_exec` | A Python snippet in a sandbox |
| `__function__:end_call` | Hangs up. Used in the `terminal` of an `end_call` node |

Handlers for integrations, knowledge search, call transfer and rescheduling also exist. They are not needed here.

`api_call` parameters:

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `url` | Request URL. `{{var}}` works |
| `method` | HTTP method |
| `headers` | Object. Each header is a property with a `default` |
| `body` | Object. Each body field is a property under `body.properties` |
| `connect_retries` | Transport retries. See "Retries and timeouts" |

## How a parameter gets its value

One key decides, per parameter: `default`.

| Declaration | Who supplies the value | Does the model see the parameter |
|---|---|---|
| `default` with a literal, or with a `{{var}}` that has a value | The workflow. The value is **baked** | No |
| `default` with a `{{var}}` that has no value when the node is entered | The model | Yes, named after the variable, with the property's `type`, `description` and `enum` |
| no `default` | The model | Yes |
| `const` | Nobody. `const` does **not** bake | It only constrains the model's own output |

Rules:

- **Use `default` for fixed backend config** such as `url`, `method` and auth headers. At registration the engine moves every `default` into the tool's base config, resolves `{{var}}` from the variable table, and removes the field from the schema the model sees.
- **Never use `const` for a value you want sent.** The engine reads only `default`. A `{{var}}` inside a `const` never resolves. An `api_call` whose `url` is a `const` fails with "URL is required".
- **Baking happens when the node is entered.** A `{{var}}` default is resolved against the variable table at that moment.

The working builder uses this for every tool: `customer_id` has `"default": "{{customer_id}}"` and is baked from a call variable. Every other body field has `"default": "{{<field name>}}"`, where no variable of that name exists, so the model fills it. Verified in a working builder.

Seen in a trial call: the model's arguments are stored as `<tool>_args.<field>` in the variable table, for example `lookup_order_args.order_number`. They were not stored under the bare field name.

Take care that a model-filled field does not share its name with a variable that is already set when the node is entered. The value would be baked and the model would never see the parameter.

### `api_call` body field rules

- Declare each body field as a leaf under `body.properties.<field>`.
- Put the field's `type`, `description` and `enum` on that leaf. Put required fields in `body.required`.
- Give each leaf its own `default`.
- Do not put a field spec at the top level of `parameters.properties` next to a `body.default` template object. The engine looks for the spec at `body.properties.<field>`, does not find it, and the model sees only "Template variable: name". The `enum` and `description` are lost while the call still works.
- A body that exists only as one `body.default` object also shows as an empty form in the dashboard editor. Saving from there removes the tool.

A `code_exec` tool is different: its parameters are true top-level arguments. Declare a model-filled one as a top-level property without `default`.

### When a baked variable has no value

| Field type | Variable unset | Variable is `""` |
|---|---|---|
| Normal field in an engine-run call (`pre_actions`, lifecycle tool) | The field is dropped from the request. No error | The field is sent empty |
| `code` of `code_exec` | The literal text `{{var}}` stays in the Python source and the snippet crashes | |

Fix: make sure an earlier node always sets the variable, even to a sentinel value. In code, read variables from `vars` and do not splice them in with `{{var}}`.

### Constrain model-filled parameters

When a value must be one of a known set, do not use a free string. The model sometimes invents a value that looks plausible.

- Use an `enum` on the leaf, and list the values in the `description` as well.
- Or use a `number` that is an index into a list, with the valid range in the description. A pre-hook or the backend turns the index into the real value.
- If neither is possible, name the exact source in the description and tell the model to copy the value unchanged.

```json
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "queue": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "Team that takes over. One of: billing, delivery, returns.",
      "enum": ["billing", "delivery", "returns"],
      "default": "{{queue}}"
    }
  },
  "required": ["queue"]
}
```

## `pre_actions` versus `tools`

The placement decides who fires the call.

| Placement | Node type | Who calls it | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pre_actions` | `api_request`, `code` | The engine | On node entry, before any model turn |
| `tools` | `conversation` | The dialogue model | During a turn, when the model decides to |
| Workflow-level `tools` with `config.alwaysRunsAt` | none | The engine | At call start or call end |

The platform removes `tools` from non-conversation nodes and `pre_actions` from conversation nodes. It does so without an error: the JSON you sent looks fine, the create call succeeds, and the stored node has an empty array. A node cannot use both.

**Use `pre_actions`** when the call must always run and the model has nothing to decide. Example: after the order number is known, always fetch the order.

**Use `tools`** when the call depends on what the user says. Example: cancel the order only if the caller asks for it.

Differences in behaviour:

| | `pre_actions` | `tools` |
|---|---|---|
| Can be skipped | No | Yes. The model may not call it if the description and the prompt do not push for it |
| Timing | Node entry | Inside a turn. The model can call a tool, speak, then call another |
| Result in the conversation | A tool call and tool result pair is added to the history | The same |
| `response_mapping` lives | On the **node** | On the **tool** |
| `description` | Ignored | The only text the model reads about the tool |

To run a fixed call before a tool-driven conversation, use a passthrough `api_request` node and transition from it into the conversation node. Do not build a long chain of passthrough nodes for optional actions. Put those into one conversation node with several tools.

### A `pre_actions` node

```json
{
  "name": "fetch_order",
  "node_type": "api_request",
  "passthrough": true,
  "passthrough_default_transition": "present",
  "on_enter": { "type": "silent" },
  "pre_actions": [
    {
      "type": "function",
      "config": { "timeoutMs": 10000, "maxRetries": 2 },
      "function": {
        "name": "get_order",
        "handler": "__function__:api_call",
        "description": "Get the order.",
        "parameters": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": {
            "url": { "type": "string", "default": "https://api.example.com/v1/get_order" },
            "method": { "type": "string", "default": "POST" },
            "headers": { "type": "object", "properties": { "Content-Type": { "type": "string", "default": "application/json" } } },
            "body": { "type": "object", "properties": { "order_number": { "type": "string", "default": "{{order_number}}" } }, "required": [] }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "response_mapping": [
    { "path": "data.items", "variable": "items" }
  ],
  "transitions": [
    { "target_node": "present", "description": "always", "condition": { "operator": "always" } }
  ]
}
```

The last `always` transition is mandatory. A passthrough node with no matching transition deadlocks.

### Tool descriptions

In `tools`, the `description` decides whether the model calls the tool.

- Write it as an instruction with the trigger: "CALL it every time the caller gives an order number."
- A plain description such as "Looks up an order" lets the model acknowledge the request in words and never call the tool. That is the most common failure of nodes with many tools.
- If two tools could match, say which one not to use and name the other.
- In `task_message`, put the tool rules before long reference text and state: when a rule says to use a tool, call the tool.
- The working builder also tells the model to call one tool per message and to speak after every tool result. Verified in a working builder. In a trial call a model turn with no text and no tool call produced the error event "The model returned no speakable content".

A tool is available only in the nodes that list it. Seen in a trial call: the model called a tool that the current node did not list. The result was the text "The function `<name>` is not currently available."

## `response_mapping`

`response_mapping` copies values from a call result into named variables. It needs no model call.

```json
{
  "response_mapping": [
    { "path": "data.status", "variable": "order_status" },
    { "path": "data.items", "variable": "items" }
  ]
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `path` | Dot path into the tool result |
| `variable` | Name of the variable to set |

### Placement

- For a tool in `tools`: inside the tool object, next to `function` and `config`.
- For `pre_actions`: at the **node level**. A `response_mapping` nested inside a `pre_actions` entry is ignored and the variable never appears.

`extraction_schema` follows the same placement rule if you use it on a call result.

### Where a result lands (trial findings)

Seen in a trial call: the result of an `api_call` is an envelope around the HTTP response.

```json
{
  "status": "success",
  "data": { "ok": true, "verified": true, "attempts_left": 3 },
  "message": "Successfully executed POST request",
  "status_code": 200,
  "header": { "Content-Type": "application/json" }
}
```

`data` is the JSON body the API returned. `header` holds the HTTP response headers.

The engine also writes every result into the variable table by itself, flattened with dots. You do not need a mapping for these. For a tool named `check_answer` whose API returned `{"ok": true, "verified": true, "attempts_left": 3}`, the trial call's variable table held:

| Variable | Value |
|---|---|
| `check_answer_args.<field>` | Each argument the model sent |
| `check_answer_response.status` | `success` |
| `check_answer_response.data.ok` | `true` (a string) |
| `check_answer_response.data.verified` | `true` (a string) |
| `check_answer_response.data.attempts_left` | `3` |
| `check_answer_response.message` | `Successfully executed POST request` |
| `check_answer_response.status_code` | `200` |
| `check_answer_response.header.<Header-Name>` | One variable per response header |
| `check_answer_status_code` | `200` |
| `check_answer_success_count` | Number of successful calls so far |

Each call of the same tool overwrites the previous `_args` and `_response` values.

### Which mapping paths work

- **Start the path at the envelope, with `data.`**. If the API returns `{"ok": true}`, map `data.ok`. If it returns `{"products": [...]}`, map `data.products`. Verified in a working builder, on a tool-level mapping and on a node-level mapping.
- A path without the `data.` prefix (for the same body: `ok`) is not confirmed. A smaller example builder uses it. In an early trial call the mapped variables stayed unset and the transitions on them never fired. The mapping paths of that call are not recorded. The builder that passed uses `data.` paths.
- The flattened key can be used directly as a transition variable: `check_answer_response.data.verified`. Verified in a working builder, which tests the mapped variable and the flattened key in the same OR group as a safeguard.
- Booleans arrive as strings. The trial call showed `true` in lower case in the flattened keys. Test both `"true"` and `"True"`, or map a string field.
- A mapped list or object: the exact form it has later inside `vars` is not confirmed. The working builder reads it defensively. It accepts a list, a JSON string, and flattened keys.

## Routing on tool results

Routing runs again after a tool result arrives. A transition on a result variable fires in the same turn, before any further model turn. Seen in a trial call.

```json
{
  "transitions": [
    {
      "target_node": "load_order",
      "description": "The check passed",
      "condition": {
        "logic": "or",
        "conditions": [
          { "variable": "check_passed", "operator": "equals", "operand": "true" },
          { "variable": "check_passed", "operator": "equals", "operand": "True" },
          { "variable": "check_answer_response.data.verified", "operator": "equals", "operand": "true" },
          { "variable": "check_answer_response.data.verified", "operator": "equals", "operand": "True" }
        ]
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

Rules:

- On a passthrough node, end with an `always` transition so that a failed or empty response does not deadlock.
- Use a tool result to leave a conversation node. The pattern "a closing tool sets a variable, a transition on that variable leads to an `end_call` node" is verified in a working builder.
- To leave a node that carries out an action, do not re-test the user's earlier intent with `matches_intent`. The router looks at the latest user message and can route away before the tool was called. Extract a follow-up enum with a default such as `stay`, and branch with `equals`.

### Success and failure counters

The engine keeps two integer variables per call target. No mapping is needed.

| Placement | Variables |
|---|---|
| `pre_actions` node | `<nodeId>_success_count`, `<nodeId>_failure_count` |
| Tool in `tools` with handler `api_call` | `<toolName>_success_count`, `<toolName>_failure_count` |

Seen in a trial call: `check_answer_success_count` was `2` after two successful calls, and a code node named `setup` produced `setup_success_count` with the value `1`.

```json
{
  "transitions": [
    { "target_node": "give_up", "description": "The lookup failed three times", "condition": { "logic": "or", "conditions": [ { "variable": "lookup_order_failure_count", "operator": "greater_than", "operand": 2 } ] } },
    { "target_node": "ask_again", "description": "always", "condition": { "operator": "always" } }
  ]
}
```

### `suppress_tool_results`

A node-level boolean for nodes that run API calls. With `true` the dialogue model sees only a short `{status: "success"}` summary in place of the raw response. Variables are still mapped and routing still sees them. Use it for large responses, or when the mapped variables already hold everything the model needs.

### Background tools

A tool with `"config": {"interruptible": false}` runs in the background. A user interruption does not cancel it. Its result arrives one or more turns later. The mapped variables, the `_response` keys and the counters are filled as usual, but not in the same turn. A transition that reads them right after the call can find them unset. Gate on the variable with `is_set`.

## Retries and timeouts

| Setting | Where | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `timeoutMs` | `config` | not documented | Time limit of one attempt, in milliseconds |
| `maxRetries` | `config` | not documented | Tool-level retries after a failed response |
| `connect_retries` | `parameters.properties`, as a baked parameter | `2` | Retries when the connection could not be established |
| `timeout_ms` | `code_exec` parameter | `30000` | Time limit of a code snippet |

`connect_retries` in detail:

- It retries only failures to establish the connection: connection refused, or reset during the TCP or TLS handshake. The request never reached the server, so a repeat is safe even for POST.
- HTTP error statuses and timeouts are not retried by it.
- Hard cap `5`. `0` means a single attempt.
- Back-off is 150 ms times the attempt number, with a new connection each time.
- All attempts share one 30 second budget for the request.
- Declare it next to `url` and `method`: `"connect_retries": {"type": "number", "default": 0}`. It is not a `config` field.

The working builder sets `maxRetries` to `0` on tools that write data and to `2` on its read-only `pre_actions` call. A retried write can record the same thing twice if the API is not idempotent.

## Pre and post Python hooks

An `api_call` tool can carry two Python snippets. They run on the server, in a sandbox, right before and right after the call. They are top-level fields of the tool object.

```json
{
  "type": "function",
  "config": { "timeoutMs": 10000, "maxRetries": 0 },
  "function": {
    "name": "check_answer",
    "handler": "__function__:api_call",
    "description": "Check one answer. CALL it every time the caller answers the question.",
    "parameters": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "url": { "type": "string", "default": "https://api.example.com/v1/check_answer" },
        "method": { "type": "string", "default": "POST" },
        "body": { "type": "object", "properties": { "answer": { "type": "string", "description": "The caller's answer", "default": "{{answer}}" } }, "required": ["answer"] }
      }
    }
  },
  "pre_process_code": "vars['member_code'] = str(vars.get('member_code') or '').strip().upper()",
  "post_process_code": "try:\n    if isinstance(result, dict):\n        result.pop('header', None)\n        d = result.get('data')\n        if isinstance(d, dict):\n            d['what_to_do_next'] = 'Ask the next question.' if d.get('verified') else 'Ask the same question again.'\nexcept Exception:\n    pass\n"
}
```

| Hook | Names available | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `pre_process_code` | `vars`: mutable dict that fills the `{{var}}` placeholders of the request. `config`: the substituted request with `url`, `method`, `headers`, `body` | Clean a value, or rewrite the whole request |
| `post_process_code` | `result`: the tool result, mutable | Reshape, shorten or extend the result |

Documented behaviour:

- The post-hook runs before `response_mapping` and extraction see the result.
- An empty or whitespace-only string means no hook.
- Hooks are honoured only on `api_call` tools (and on the integration and knowledge search handlers). The platform removes them from any other handler when the workflow is saved.
- In a pre-hook, setting `config['body']` to a string sends that string as the raw body, with no JSON encoding. Set the `Content-Type` header yourself in that case.

### What `result` looks like in a post-hook

The internal reference shows `result` as the response body. A working builder shows otherwise. Verified in a working builder:

- For an `api_call`, `result` is the envelope described above: a dict with `status`, `data`, `message`, `status_code` and `header`. The API's JSON body is `result["data"]`.
- A key that the hook adds inside `result["data"]` reaches the dialogue model as part of the tool result. The working builder adds a `what_to_do_next` sentence there, and its prompt tells the model to obey it.
- `result.pop("header", None)` removes the response headers. The working builder does this on every tool, so that headers do not take up space in the model's context.
- Mapping paths still start with `data.` when a post-hook is present.

The working builder writes every hook inside `try` and `except Exception: pass` and checks types with `isinstance` before use. What the platform does when a hook raises is not documented.

Seen in a test on 10 October: a post-hook can read call variables and write new variables, and a later pre-hook reads them. Not confirmed: whether a change to `result` also changes the flattened `<tool>_response.*` variables.

## Code nodes and `code_exec`

A `code` node runs a Python snippet when it is entered. The snippet is a `code_exec` function in `pre_actions`.

```json
{
  "name": "compute_delivery",
  "node_type": "code",
  "passthrough": true,
  "passthrough_default_transition": "tell_delivery",
  "on_enter": { "type": "silent" },
  "pre_actions": [
    {
      "type": "function",
      "function": {
        "name": "code_exec",
        "handler": "__function__:code_exec",
        "parameters": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": {
            "code": { "type": "string", "default": "import datetime\ntry:\n    start = datetime.date.fromisoformat(str(vars.get('shipped_on'))[:10])\n    eta = start + datetime.timedelta(days=3)\n    vars['delivery_day'] = eta.isoformat()\n    vars['delivery_state'] = 'known'\nexcept Exception:\n    vars['delivery_day'] = ''\n    vars['delivery_state'] = 'unknown'\n" },
            "timeout_ms": { "type": "number", "default": 10000 }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "transitions": [
    { "target_node": "tell_delivery", "description": "always", "condition": { "operator": "always" } }
  ]
}
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `code` | The Python source, as a baked `default` string |
| `timeout_ms` | Time limit in milliseconds. Default `30000` |

### Reading and writing variables

- The snippet gets a dict named `vars`. It holds the current workflow variables.
- Read with `vars.get("name")`. A variable that was never set is absent.
- Write with `vars["name"] = value`. Every key the snippet assigns becomes a workflow variable.

Verified in a working builder:

- Call variables are in `vars`. The builder reads `vars.get("now")`, a call variable passed with the simulation.
- The result of an earlier `api_request` node is reachable from `vars` in a later code node. The builder looks for it under the mapped variable name first and under the flattened result keys second. Which of the two held the data is not recorded.
- A string written to `vars["date_facts"]` in a code node resolves as `{{date_facts}}` in the `task_message` of later conversation nodes. Multi-line strings work.
- The standard modules `json`, `re` and `datetime` can be imported.
- The same snippet can run in two code nodes at different points of the call. The later run sees the variables added in between.

### What a code node returns

Seen in a trial call: the result of a successful `code_exec` is

```json
{ "status": "success", "data": null, "message": "Code executed successfully", "status_code": 200 }
```

The snippet's output is not in `data`. Its values reach the workflow only through `vars`. After a code node named `setup` ran, the variable table held:

| Variable | Value |
|---|---|
| each key the snippet wrote, for example `date_facts` | the value, with source `tool_result` and source node `setup` |
| `setup_response.status` | `success` |
| `setup_response.data` | `null` |
| `setup_response.message` | `Code executed successfully` |
| `setup_response.status_code` | `200` |
| `setup_status_code` | `200` |
| `setup_success_count` | `1` |

For a code node the automatic keys are named after the **node**, not after `code_exec`.

### Rules for snippets

- **Do not write `{{` or `}}` in the code.** The internal sources disagree on whether the `code` field is templated. One says it is exempt. Another says placeholders are resolved when the code runs and an unset one is left as literal text, which breaks the Python. The working builder removes every `{{` and `}}` from generated code (a nested dict literal such as `{'a': {'b': 1}}` ends in `}}`) and reads all values from `vars`.
- **Never let a snippet raise.** Wrap the body in `try` and `except`, and write a fallback value for every variable that a later prompt or condition reads. A prompt that references an unset variable shows the literal placeholder to the model.
- **Write strings for routing flags**, such as `known` and `unknown`. Do not route on a Python boolean. See "Do not route on a boolean" in workflow-format.md.
- Keep snippets fast. They block the conversation.
- Do arithmetic, date calculation and counting in code, and give the model the finished facts as text. Verified in a working builder: it computes a block of date facts in a code node and places it in the prompts.
- Treat a code node like an API node: `passthrough: true`, a `passthrough_default_transition`, and a last `always` transition.

### Sandbox limits

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Time | `timeout_ms`, default `30000` |
| Modules | `json`, `re` and `datetime` are verified in a working builder. The full list is not documented |
| Network and file access | Not documented |
| Memory and output size | Not documented |

### `code_exec` as a tool

`code_exec` can also be a tool in the `tools` array of a conversation node, called by the model. Its parameters are top-level arguments, declared without `default` so the model fills them. For such a tool the `code` field resolves `{{var}}` when the tool is called, against the current variable table. The working builder does not use this form, so nothing about it is verified here.

## Lifecycle tools

A tool whose `config.alwaysRunsAt` is a non-empty list is never shown to the model. The engine fires it at a fixed point of the call.

| Value | When |
|---|---|
| `start_of_call` | During call setup, before the first turn |
| `end_of_call` | After the call has ended |
| `each_turn` | Accepted by the schema but not implemented. It never fires |

Put a lifecycle tool that must run on every call into the workflow's top-level `tools` array.

```json
{
  "initial_node": "greeting",
  "nodes": {},
  "tools": [
    {
      "type": "function",
      "config": { "alwaysRunsAt": ["end_of_call"] },
      "function": {
        "name": "push_call_result",
        "handler": "__function__:api_call",
        "parameters": {
          "type": "object",
          "properties": {
            "url": { "type": "string", "default": "https://api.example.com/v1/call-results" },
            "method": { "type": "string", "default": "POST" },
            "body": {
              "type": "object",
              "properties": {
                "summary": { "type": "string", "default": "{{call.analysis.summary}}" },
                "reason": { "type": "string", "default": "{{call.call_end_reason}}" }
              }
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

Rules:

- A workflow-level tool without `alwaysRunsAt` never runs and the model never sees it.
- A lifecycle tool in a node's `tools` runs for `start_of_call` only on the `initial_node`, and for `end_of_call` only on the node in which the call ended.
- If a `{{var}}` parameter is still unresolved, one model call fills the parameters. If everything resolves, the handler runs directly.
- `response_mapping` is applied for `start_of_call`. It is not applied for `end_of_call`.
- At the end of a call the order is: call analysis, then `end_of_call` tools, then success-criteria judging. An `end_of_call` tool can use `{{call.analysis.summary}}`, `{{call.analysis.structured_data_str}}`, `{{call.call_end_reason}}`, `{{call.call_end_reason_category}}`, `{{call.call_tags}}` and `{{call.duration}}`.
- A malformed lifecycle tool is dropped at run time without an error. Validate with a dry run (api.md).

## Tool results and the next turn

After a tool call returns, the model sees the result and has to produce the next turn itself. Two things were seen in practice runs with the hackathon's agent model:

- **The agent says nothing after the tool call.** The result arrives, no assistant message follows, and the simulated customer hangs up after waiting. It happens more often when the result is bare data such as `{"ok": true, "verified": true}`.
- **The agent ignores a negative result.** For example it reads `"verified": false` and moves on to the next question as if the answer had passed.

What fixed both in a working builder (verified, see the post-hook section above): a post-hook on the tool that adds one plain instruction line to the result before the model sees it, for example a `what_to_do_next` field that says what the answer means and what to say or call next. The model then has something to act on.

Also say it in the step's prompt: after every tool result, speak to the customer or call the next tool. Never end a turn with nothing.

## Checklist

- Fixed values use `default`, never `const`.
- Each `api_call` body field is a leaf under `body.properties` with its own `default`, `description` and `enum`.
- `tools` only on `conversation` nodes. `pre_actions` only on `api_request` and `code` nodes.
- `response_mapping` on the tool for `tools`, on the node for `pre_actions`.
- Mapping paths start with `data.`.
- Booleans from results are tested as `"true"` and `"True"`, or replaced by string fields.
- Every passthrough node ends with an `always` transition.
- Code reads and writes through `vars`, never raises, and contains no `{{` or `}}`.
- Tool descriptions say when to call the tool.

- v1: first release.

You write a **builder**: a program that reads a bank's brief and creates a phone agent on Freya.
We put that phone agent in front of simulated customers. The share it handles correctly is your score.

One simulated customer is one case. A step of a phone agent is called a node in the platform's documents.

## The ten-minute start

You need Python 3.10 or newer.

```bash
cp env.example env.sh        # put your Freya API key in it, and a team key you make up
source env.sh

# 1. Put the example agent on Freya and test it. It prints {"workflow_id": ..., "agent_id": ...}
python3 -c "import freya,json; print(freya.save_workflow('base', json.load(open('examples/base-agent.json'))))"
python3 tools/run_cases.py <agent_id> --brief A            # ten practice customers, 3 to 11 minutes

# 2. Let the example builder build one from the brief
pip install claude-agent-sdk
python3 examples/agent_builder.py briefs/brief-a.md
python3 examples/agent_builder.py briefs/brief-a.md briefs/brief-b.md   # Brief B builds on Brief A, so pass both
```

`run_cases.py` prints one line per customer: pass or fail, the tool calls the agent made, and the reason for a failure.

`examples/base-agent.json` is an agent, not a builder. It is the same two-step workflow that is already in your workspace: check identity, then take a payment promise. It uses four of the seven tools, so it handles only the simplest customers: in one run it passed 2 of the 13 practice customers. Read it to see what a valid workflow looks like.

`examples/agent_builder.py` is a builder. It runs Claude through the Claude Agent SDK with one skill, `.claude/skills/build-phone-agent/SKILL.md`. Claude reads the brief and the tool API file, writes the workflow, runs the practice customers and fixes what fails. The skill is short on purpose. Your job is a better builder: a better skill, more skills, your own code, or another agent altogether. It needs a Claude login or `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.

## What is in this kit

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|

## How you are scored

A customer counts as handled when all of these hold:

1. **Outcome: the bank's records are right.** The outcome, every promise (product, amount, date), every note, callback and transfer match what the brief requires. The scorer reads them from the bank, not from what the agent said.
2. **Policy: the conversation stayed inside the brief.**
3. **Honesty: the phone agent told the customer the truth**, for example it never says a promise is recorded when the tool call failed.

A judge model reads the transcript for 2 and 3, against the checks listed for that customer.

There is no partial credit. Your score is the share of customers handled.

The same phone agent can pass a customer in one run and fail it in the next. Treat one green run as a hint, not as proof.

## The final

- On Sunday we publish briefs you have not seen. They are the same kind of call with different rules: other numbers and limits, other identity questions, another outcome table, another calendar. Their form can differ too: one final brief is a clean specification, the other is raw bank material (a mail, a policy extract, a memo that changes it, a code list).
- Each final brief comes with its own tool API file. The seven tool names stay the same. The fields and the allowed values can change.
- After the final briefs open you may fix a bug in your builder. You may not write anything from a final brief into it: no rule, no value, no name. Fixing a crash on a table your parser did not expect is allowed. Adding the new brief's holiday dates or outcome names to your code or prompts is not.
- You run your builder once on each, with no manual step, and submit the phone agents it created, your code and the builder's trace.
- You export each phone agent to a file with `freya.export_workflow(workflow_id, "<brief>.workflow.json")` and submit those files. We load them into our own workspace to test them, so what you export is what we score.
- We test those phone agents on customers nobody has seen, on several calendar days, three times each. A customer counts only when all three runs pass. A phone agent that is right most of the time is not right.
- Final customers can have up to three products, as in Brief B.
- Final customers talk like people. They give a number in two parts, correct themselves, talk about other things, ask a question back, or say amounts and dates in words. The facts stay the same. Practise with `--style pieces`, `corrects`, `talkative`, `asks_back` or `in_words` on `run_cases.py`.

So build something that reads a brief, not something that knows this one. Whatever your builder can take from the brief, it should take from the brief.

## Rules

- Your builder takes brief files as input and creates the phone agent with no manual step. Do not edit a phone agent by hand after it is created.
- The phone agent runs on the model set in `freya.py` (`AGENT_LLM`). Do not change it. Your builder may use any model or coding agent.
- The phone agent may call only the bank's tool API. Code steps and hooks inside the workflow are allowed and expected.
- Use `freya.save_workflow(...)` or update your workflow in place. A workspace holds 200 workflows. A builder that creates a new one on every run fills it up and leaves you with a list nobody can read.
- One simulation runs at a time per workspace. A ten-customer run takes 3 to 11 minutes. A second `run_cases.py` started meanwhile waits for the first.
- A builder run on one brief may take 30 minutes at most, including any test it runs on its own phone agent. You may run it more than once and submit the phone agent of one run, with that run's trace.
- Equal scores are ranked by the total promised amount on the customers that passed, then by shorter build time, then by earlier submission.
- Your builder must leave a trace of each run: start and end time, each model call it made (model and a one-line purpose), what it created on Freya, and any test it ran on its own agent. Plain text, no fixed format. You submit one trace per final brief.
- All data here is synthetic. Do not bring real customer data.

## When something does not work

- `error code: 1010` in an HTML page: your request has no browser-like `User-Agent`. `freya.py` sets one.
- `Workspace plan limit reached`: you created too many workflows. Update one in place.
- You changed your builder and the score did not move at all: an updated workflow must be published before a simulation uses it. `freya.save_workflow` publishes. A plain `PUT` does not. See "Update a workflow" in `docs/api.md`.
- A customer fails and you do not see why: `freya.get_call(call_id)["messages"]` is the full transcript with the tool calls. `run_cases.py --out results/run.json` saves the call id of every customer.
- Calls end as `customer-ended-call` before the phone agent is done: it was silent too long and the customer hung up, as a person would. `run_cases.py` prints the slowest agent turn per call after every run, and a warning when the median is above 10 seconds. If the same phone agent is fast in the next run, the model was busy and the low score was not yours.
- You want to see what your phone agent says without waiting for a simulation: `POST /api/v2/chat/message` runs one turn at a time. See `docs/api.md`.
- The bank answers `unknown product_id`: the model made an id up. Product ids come from `get_account` (`p1`, `p2`, ...). Give them to the model in the tool result, or fill them in with code.
- A simulation stays at "running" and no call ever starts: the workflow cannot start a call. Try one chat turn. Leave `agent_config` out of the workflow you send.
- The agent says nothing after a tool call and the customer hangs up: see "Tool results and the next turn" in `docs/tools-and-code.md`.
"""Thin client for the Freya API. Standard library only.

    export FREYA_API_KEY=fak_...            # your workspace key
    export FREYA_API_URL=https://staging-app.freyavoice.ai   # default
"""
import json, os, time, urllib.request, urllib.error, urllib.parse

URL = os.environ.get("FREYA_API_URL", "https://staging-app.freyavoice.ai")
# Cloudflare rejects requests without a browser-like User-Agent (error 1010).
HEADERS = {"Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ.get("FREYA_API_KEY", ""), "Content-Type": "application/json", "User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (build-the-builder)"}

def api(method, path, body=None, **params):
    """Call the API and return the `result` part of its {success, data: {message, result}} envelope."""
    q = "?" + urllib.parse.urlencode(params) if params else ""
    req = urllib.request.Request(URL + path + q, data=json.dumps(body).encode() if body is not None else None, headers=HEADERS, method=method)
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=120) as r: out = json.load(r)
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{method} {path} -> {e.code}: {e.read().decode()[:1500]}") from None
    return out.get("data", {}).get("result", out) if isinstance(out, dict) else out

_ws = None
def workspace_id():
    """The workspace your key belongs to. List routes need it as a query parameter."""
    global _ws
    if not _ws:
        r = api("GET", "/api/v2/workspaces"); items = r.get("workspaces") or r.get("items") or r
        _ws = os.environ.get("FREYA_WORKSPACE_ID") or items[0]["id"]
    return _ws

def create_workflow(name, workflow):
    """Create a workflow. Freya creates its agent with it. Returns {workflow_id, agent_id}."""
    w = api("POST", "/api/v2/workflow", {"name": name, "workflow": workflow})["workflow"]
    return {"workflow_id": w["id"], "agent_id": w["agentId"]}

def save_workflow(slot, workflow, state_file=".freya-agents.json"):
    """Create the workflow the first time, update the same one afterwards. Use this in your builder.

    `slot` is your own label, for example the brief's file name. A workspace holds a limited number of workflows,
    so a builder that creates a new one on every run stops working after a few runs."""
    import pathlib
    f = pathlib.Path(state_file); state = json.loads(f.read_text()) if f.exists() else {}
    if slot in state:
        state[slot]["version"] = update_workflow(state[slot]["workflow_id"], workflow); f.write_text(json.dumps(state, indent=1))
    else:
        state[slot] = create_workflow(f"{slot} {time.strftime('%m%d-%H%M%S')}", workflow); f.write_text(json.dumps(state, indent=1))
    return state[slot]
def validate_workflow(name, workflow): return api("POST", "/api/v2/workflow", {"name": name, "workflow": workflow}, dryRun="true")
def update_workflow(workflow_id, workflow):
    """Update a workflow and publish the new version. Returns the published version number.

    An update alone only saves a new, unpublished version. Simulations and calls keep running the published one,
    so an update that is not published tests your old phone agent."""
    api("PUT", f"/api/v2/workflow/{workflow_id}", {"workflow": workflow})
    # The platform fills in a default agent_config. If its model is not the event's model, a simulation still runs
    # (it overrides the model), but a chat turn or a real call cannot start. Set the model and save once more.
    w = api("GET", f"/api/v2/workflow/{workflow_id}", workspaceId=workspace_id())["workflow"]["workflow"]
    ac = w.get("agent_config") or {}; llm = ac.get("llmConfig") or {}
    if (llm.get("provider"), llm.get("model")) != (AGENT_LLM["provider"], AGENT_LLM["model"]):
        ac["llmConfig"] = {**llm, **AGENT_LLM}; api("PUT", f"/api/v2/workflow/{workflow_id}", {"workflow": {**w, "agent_config": ac}})
    vs = api("GET", f"/api/v2/versions/workflow/{workflow_id}", workspaceId=workspace_id())["versions"]
    newest = max(vs, key=lambda v: v["versionNumber"])
    if not newest.get("isPublished"): api("POST", f"/api/v2/versions/workflow/{workflow_id}/publish", {"versionId": newest["id"]})
    return newest["versionNumber"]
def export_workflow(workflow_id, path):
    """Write the workflow as it is on the platform to a file. This file is part of what you submit."""
    w = api("GET", f"/api/v2/workflow/{workflow_id}", workspaceId=workspace_id())["workflow"]
    open(path, "w").write(json.dumps({"workflow_id": w["id"], "agent_id": w.get("agentId"), "updated_at": w.get("updatedAt"), "workflow": w["workflow"]}, indent=1)); return path
def create_personas(personas):        return api("POST", "/api/v2/personas", {"personas": personas})
def get_iteration(sim_id, it_id):
    """One iteration with ALL its runs. The route returns 30 runs by default and 100 at most, so this reads page by page."""
    out, off = None, 0
    while True:
        r = api("GET", f"/api/v2/simulations/{sim_id}/iterations/{it_id}", limit=100, offset=off)
        if out is None: out = r
        else: out["runs"] += r["runs"]
        off += 100
        if len(r["runs"]) < 100: return out
def get_call(call_id):
    """One simulated call: `messages` holds the transcript, tool calls included. Run ids and call ids come from get_iteration()['runs']."""
    return api("GET", f"/api/v2/call/{call_id}")["call"]

# The model every team's phone agent runs on: Freya's model on the event's own GPU box. Do not change it. (Organisers can point a test at another model with the two variables.)
AGENT_LLM = {"provider": os.environ.get("FREYA_AGENT_PROVIDER", "experimental-5"), "model": os.environ.get("FREYA_AGENT_MODEL", "experimental-5")}
SIM_LLM = {"provider": "google", "model": "gemini-3-flash-preview"}        # plays the customer and judges

def run_simulation(agent_id, name, variables_by_persona, max_seconds=420, concurrency=int(os.environ.get("FREYA_SIM_CONCURRENCY", "5"))):
    """Start a text simulation, wait for it, return (simulation_id, iteration_id)."""
    while True:                      # a workspace runs one simulation at a time: wait for the running one instead of failing
        try:
            sim = api("POST", "/api/v2/simulations", {
                "agentId": agent_id, "name": name, "mode": "chat", "selectedPersonaIds": list(variables_by_persona),
                "customerVariablesMap": variables_by_persona, "maxConcurrentCalls": concurrency, "runsPerPersona": 1, "maxCallDurationSeconds": max_seconds,
                "assistantLlmOverride": AGENT_LLM, "routingLlmOverride": AGENT_LLM, "extractionLlmOverride": AGENT_LLM,
                "personaLlmOverride": SIM_LLM, "analysisLlmOverride": SIM_LLM})
            break
        except RuntimeError as e:
            if "concurrent simulations" not in str(e): raise
            print("another simulation is running in this workspace, waiting 30 s", flush=True); time.sleep(30)
    sim_id = (sim.get("simulation") or sim)["id"]
    while True:
        time.sleep(10)
        s = api("GET", f"/api/v2/simulations/{sim_id}"); s = s.get("simulation") or s
        if s.get("status") in ("completed", "failed", "paused"): break
    its = api("GET", f"/api/v2/simulations/{sim_id}/iterations"); its = its.get("iterations") or its.get("items") or its
    return sim_id, its[0]["id"], s.get("status")
"""Run cases against an agent and score them from the bank's ledger and the judge's reading of the conversation.

    python tools/run_cases.py <agent_id> [--brief A|B] [--cases public-test-set.json] [--out results/run.json] [--reps 3] [--style talkative]

Needs FREYA_API_KEY (your workspace) and FREYA_BANK_TEAM_KEY (any secret of 16+ characters your team picks, the same one every time).
"""
import argparse, hashlib, json, os, pathlib, sys, time
ROOT = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT)); sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT / "tools"))
import freya
from score import http, score_ledger

PERSONA = """OUTPUT RULE: Write only the words you say on the phone. No stage directions, no brackets. One or two short sentences per turn, then wait for the other side.

WHO YOU ARE: {who}

WHAT HAPPENS IN THIS CALL: {script}

RULES:
- Answer what you are asked. Do not volunteer information nobody asked for.
- When you give a number or a date, say all of it in one turn. Never stop halfway through.
- Do not invent dates, amounts or facts that are not written above. If asked something that is not covered, give a short neutral answer.
- If the caller reads something back and it matches what you agreed, say "Yes, I confirm."
- When the caller says goodbye, say "Thank you, goodbye." and say nothing more."""

# How a customer talks. The facts of the case stay the same, only the way of saying them changes.
STYLES = {
    "pieces": "HOW YOU TALK: you give long numbers and dates in two parts. Say the first half, stop, and give the rest in your next turn or when asked. This replaces the rule about saying all of it in one turn.",
    "corrects": "HOW YOU TALK: the first time you say a day or an amount, you say a slightly different one first and correct yourself in the same sentence, like 'the 21st, sorry, I mean the 20th'. The corrected value is the one written above. Do this once or twice in the call, not more. Never do it with a security answer: those you say right the first time unless the text above says otherwise.",
    "talkative": "HOW YOU TALK: you talk a lot. Before most answers you add one or two sentences about your day, the traffic or how busy work is. Once in the call you mention that your cousin's wedding is on the 30th. It has nothing to do with any payment, and you never offer it as a payment day.",
    "asks_back": "HOW YOU TALK: twice in the call, before you answer, you ask a short question back, like 'why do you need that?' or 'which account is this about?'. Whatever the caller replies, you then give your answer.",
    "in_words": "HOW YOU TALK: you say every amount and every date in words and never in digits, like 'four hundred and fifty-five' and 'the twenty-second of October'. Postcodes, years and other codes you say digit by digit.",
}

def persona_for(case, ident, style=None):
    v, i = case["variables"], ident["identity"]
    me = f"{v['first_name']} {v['last_name']}"
    if case["family"] == "Third party" or case.get("third_party"):
        who = f"You are NOT {me}. You answered this phone. You do not know {me}'s security answers and you would not give them. The text below says who you are."
    else:
        say = {"date_of_birth": "Your date of birth is {} (say it in words, like '14 March 1988').", "phone_last4": "The last four digits of your phone number on file are {}.",
               "postcode": "The postcode of your registered address is {}.", "birth_year": "Your year of birth is {}.",
               "company_number": "Your company number is {}.", "founded_year": "The company was founded in {}."}
        who = f"You are {me}. " + " ".join(say.get(k, "Your " + k.replace("_", " ") + " is {}.").format(x) for k, x in i.items()) + " Give these only when asked, and give the wrong ones where the text below says so."
    style = style or case.get("style")
    text = PERSONA.format(who=who, script=case["script"]) + ("\n\n" + STYLES[style] if style else "")
    return {"name": case["id"] + " " + case["title"] + (f" [{style}]" if style else ""), "prompt": text, "successCriteria": "All of these are true:\n- " + "\n- ".join(case["checks"]), "tags": ["hackathon", "brief-" + case["brief"]]}

def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(); ap.add_argument("agent_id"); ap.add_argument("--brief"); ap.add_argument("--cases", default=str(ROOT / "public-test-set.json")); ap.add_argument("--out"); ap.add_argument("--only"); ap.add_argument("--reps", type=int, default=1); ap.add_argument("--style", choices=sorted(STYLES)); ap.add_argument("--rerun-if-slow", type=int, default=0)
    a = ap.parse_args()
    cases = [c for c in json.load(open(a.cases)) if (not a.brief or c["brief"] == a.brief) and (not a.only or c["id"] in a.only.split(","))]
    ident = {c["id"]: {"identity": c["identity"]} for c in cases}
    store = ROOT / ".personas.json"; ids = json.load(open(store)) if store.exists() else {}
    # a persona is recreated whenever its text changes, so an edited case never runs with a stale customer
    spec = {c["id"]: persona_for(c, ident[c["id"]], a.style) for c in cases}
    key = {i: i + ":" + hashlib.sha1(json.dumps(p, sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()[:10] for i, p in spec.items()}
    new = [c for c in cases if key[c["id"]] not in ids]
    if new:
        made = freya.create_personas([spec[c["id"]] for c in new])["personas"]
        ids.update({key[c["id"]]: p["id"] for c, p in zip(new, made)}); json.dump(ids, open(store, "w"), indent=1)
    ids = {c["id"]: ids[key[c["id"]]] for c in cases}
    (ROOT / "results").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    reps, total_s = [], 0
    for rep in range(a.reps):
        for attempt in range(1 + a.rerun_if_slow):                   # organisers: a run made while the model was slow is thrown away and repeated
            rows, sim_id, it_id, status, took, med = run_once(a.agent_id, cases, ids)
            if med <= 10 or attempt == a.rerun_if_slow: break
            print(f"-- run discarded: median slowest turn {med:.0f} s. Waiting 5 minutes, then repeating it.\n", flush=True); time.sleep(300)
        reps.append(rows); total_s += took
        if a.reps > 1: print(f"-- run {rep + 1} of {a.reps}: {sum(r['pass'] for r in rows)} / {len(rows)} passed, {took:.0f} s\n")
    need = a.reps                                                # a customer counts only when every run passes
    final = [{"id": c["id"], "family": c["family"], "passes": sum(r[k]["pass"] for r in reps), "runs": a.reps, "pass": sum(r[k]["pass"] for r in reps) >= need} for k, c in enumerate(cases)]
    n = sum(f["pass"] for f in final)
    if a.reps > 1:
        for f in final: print(("PASS" if f["pass"] else "FAIL"), f["id"], f"{f['passes']}/{f['runs']}")
    print(f"\n{n} / {len(final)} passed (bank records and conversation checks){'' if a.reps == 1 else f', a customer counts with {need} of {a.reps} runs'}. Last simulation {sim_id}, status {status}, {total_s:.0f} s.")
    with open(ROOT / "results" / "log.jsonl", "a") as f:      # one line per run, the record of how the score moved over time
        f.write(json.dumps({"at": time.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), "agent_id": a.agent_id, "brief": a.brief, "runs": a.reps, "passed": n, "total": len(final), "seconds": round(total_s), "failed": [f["id"] for f in final if not f["pass"]]}) + "\n")
    if a.out:
        pathlib.Path(a.out).parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        json.dump({"agent_id": a.agent_id, "simulation_id": sim_id, "iteration_id": it_id, "seconds": round(total_s), "passed": n, "total": len(final), "runs": a.reps, "final": final, "rows": reps[-1], "all_rows": reps}, open(a.out, "w"), indent=1)

def run_once(agent_id, cases, ids):
    """One simulation: every case once. Returns the scored rows."""
    sessions = {c["id"]: http("/v1/practice/sessions", {"case": c["id"]})["variables"] for c in cases}
    t0 = time.time()
    sim_id, it_id, status = freya.run_simulation(agent_id, f"cases {time.strftime('%H:%M:%S')}", {ids[c["id"]]: sessions[c["id"]] for c in cases})
    took = time.time() - t0
    judge = {r["personaId"]: r for r in freya.get_iteration(sim_id, it_id)["runs"]}
    rows = []
    for c in cases:
        led = http("/v1/practice/ledger/" + sessions[c["id"]]["customer_id"])
        r = score_ledger(c, led)
        j = judge.get(ids[c["id"]], {})                      # the conversation checks, read from the transcript by the judge model
        if j.get("outcome") != "pass": r["failed"].append("conversation: " + " ".join(str(j.get("reason") or "no verdict").split())[:400])
        r["pass"] = not r["failed"]
        rows.append({"id": c["id"], "level": c["level"], "family": c["family"], "pass": r["pass"], "failed": r["failed"], "call_id": j.get("callId"), "tools": [x["tool"] for x in led["calls"]], "customer_id": sessions[c["id"]]["customer_id"]})
        print(("PASS" if r["pass"] else "FAIL"), c["id"], f"{c['level']:<6}", f"{c['family']:<14}", "|", " > ".join(x["tool"].replace("verify_identity", "verify").replace("create_promise", "promise") for x in led["calls"]) or "(no tool calls)")
        for f in r["failed"]: print("       -", f[:260])
    # How long the phone agent kept the customer waiting. A call whose customer hung up after long silences says
    # something about the speed of the model at that moment, not only about the agent.
    waits = []
    for r in rows:
        if not r["call_id"]: continue
        try: call = freya.get_call(r["call_id"])
        except Exception: continue
        last_user, worst = None, 0.0
        for m in call.get("messages", []):
            t = m.get("secondsFromStart")
            if t is None: continue
            if m.get("role") == "user": last_user = t
            elif last_user is not None: worst = max(worst, t - last_user); last_user = None if m.get("role") == "assistant" else last_user
        r["slowest_turn_s"] = round(worst, 1); r["ended"] = call.get("endedReason"); waits.append(worst)
    if waits:
        waits.sort(); med = waits[len(waits) // 2]; hung = sum(r.get("ended") == "customer-ended-call" and not r["pass"] for r in rows)
        print(f"\nslowest agent turn per call: median {med:.0f} s, worst {waits[-1]:.0f} s. Failed calls where the customer hung up: {hung}.")
        if med > 10: print("WARNING: the phone agent was slow in this run. If the same agent is fast in another run, the model was busy and this score is too low.")
    return rows, sim_id, it_id, status, took, (med if waits else 0)

if __name__ == "__main__": main()
"""Score one finished session from the mock's ledger. Ledger checks only; transcript checks come from the judge.

    score_ledger(case, ledger) -> {"pass": bool, "failed": [reasons]}
"""
import json, os, sys, urllib.request

HOST = os.environ.get("FREYA_BANK_HOST", "https://freya-bank-mock.freyavoice.workers.dev")
UA = {"user-agent": "freya-bank-scorer/0.1", "content-type": "application/json"}

def http(path, body=None):
    h = dict(UA)
    h["x-team-key"] = os.environ["FREYA_BANK_TEAM_KEY"]
    req = urllib.request.Request(HOST + path, data=json.dumps(body).encode() if body is not None else None, headers=h, method="POST" if body is not None else "GET")
    try: return json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=20))
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e: return json.load(e)

def score_ledger(case, led):
    exp, bad = case["expected"], []
    got_outcome = (led.get("outcome"), led.get("reason"))
    if got_outcome != (exp["outcome"], exp.get("reason")): bad.append(f"outcome {got_outcome}, expected {(exp['outcome'], exp.get('reason'))}")
    key = lambda p: (p["product_id"], round(float(p["amount"]), 2), p["date"])
    if sorted(map(key, led["promises"])) != sorted(map(key, exp["promises"])): bad.append(f"promises {sorted(map(key, led['promises']))}, expected {sorted(map(key, exp['promises']))}")
    nk = lambda n: (n.get("product_id"), n["reason"])
    if sorted(map(nk, led["notes"])) != sorted(map(nk, exp["notes"])): bad.append(f"notes {sorted(map(nk, led['notes']))}, expected {sorted(map(nk, exp['notes']))}")
    ck = lambda c: (c["date"], c["time"])
    if sorted(map(ck, led["callbacks"])) != sorted(map(ck, exp["callbacks"])): bad.append(f"callbacks {led['callbacks']}, expected {exp['callbacks']}")
    if sorted(t["queue"] for t in led["transfers"]) != sorted(t["queue"] for t in exp["transfers"]): bad.append(f"transfers {led['transfers']}, expected {exp['transfers']}")
    calls = led["calls"]
    if not calls or calls[-1]["tool"] != "close_call": bad.append("the call was not closed with close_call")
    # policy from the ledger: tools the brief forbids before identity is verified
    for c in calls:
        if c["tool"] in ("get_account", "create_promise") and c["result"].get("error") == "identity not verified": bad.append(f"{c['tool']} called before identity was verified"); break
    if exp["outcome"] in ("not_reached", "no_contact", "unreached") and any(c["tool"] in ("verify_identity", "get_account") for c in calls): bad.append("identity or account tools used although the customer was not on the line")
    return {"pass": not bad, "failed": bad}

1	# REST API for builders
2	
3	This page lists the calls a builder needs. The workflow JSON itself is described in [workflow-format.md](workflow-format.md) and [tools-and-code.md](tools-and-code.md).
4	
5	Personas, simulations and calls are documented in full at https://docs.freyavoice.ai. Workflow creation and the workflow JSON are not documented there. Use these pages for them.
6	
7	Every call on this page is taken from a client that was run against the platform, unless a line says "not confirmed".
8	
9	## Basics
10	
11	| Item | Value |
12	|---|---|
13	| Base URL | `https://staging-app.freyavoice.ai` |
14	| Auth header | `Authorization: Bearer <your API key>`. Keys start with `fak_` |
15	| Content type | `Content-Type: application/json` |
16	| User-Agent | Required, and it must look like a browser. Example: `Mozilla/5.0 (my-builder)` |
17	
18	A request without a browser-like `User-Agent` is rejected before it reaches the API. The response is an HTML page with `error code: 1010`. Many HTTP libraries send a default agent that is rejected, so set the header yourself.
19	
20	The curl examples use these variables:
21	
22	```bash
23	export FREYA_API_URL=https://staging-app.freyavoice.ai
24	export FREYA_API_KEY=fak_your_key
25	export UA="Mozilla/5.0 (my-builder)"
26	```
27	
28	### Response envelope
29	
30	Every JSON response has this shape:
31	
32	```json
33	{
34	  "success": true,
35	  "data": {
36	    "message": "text",
37	    "result": {}
38	  }
39	}
40	```
41	
42	The payload is `data.result`. The field paths below are relative to `data.result`.
43	
44	The reference client reads the wrapper keys named below (`workflow`, `simulation`, `iterations`, `workspaces`) and falls back to the bare payload if a key is missing. Do the same in your client.
45	
46	An HTML response with status 404 means the route is wrong. Note that the workflow and call routes are singular (`/api/v2/workflow`, `/api/v2/call`) and the persona and simulation routes are plural.
47	
48	## Workflows
49	
50	### Create a workflow
51	
52	`POST /api/v2/workflow`
53	
54	The body holds a name and the workflow definition. The platform creates the agent together with the workflow.
55	
56	```bash
57	curl -s -X POST "$FREYA_API_URL/api/v2/workflow" \
58	  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FREYA_API_KEY" \
59	  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
60	  -H "User-Agent: $UA" \
61	  -d '{"name": "my agent", "workflow": {"initial_node": "start", "nodes": {}, "global_nodes": {}}}'
62	```
63	
64	| Path in `result` | Meaning |
65	|---|---|
66	| `workflow.id` | The workflow id |
67	| `workflow.agentId` | The id of the agent that was created with it. Pass this as `agentId` to a simulation |
68	
69	Put a complete workflow in `workflow`. The empty `nodes` object above only keeps the example short.
70	
71	### Validate without saving (dry run)
72	
73	`POST /api/v2/workflow?dryRun=true`
74	
75	Same body as create. The platform runs its write validation and stores nothing.
76	
77	```bash
78	curl -s -X POST "$FREYA_API_URL/api/v2/workflow?dryRun=true" \
79	  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FREYA_API_KEY" \
80	  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
81	  -H "User-Agent: $UA" \
82	  -d @request.json
83	```
84	
85	The fields of the dry-run result are not documented. The reference client treats any HTTP error status as a failure and prints the response body.
86	
87	Validation checks the schema. It also removes fields that do not belong to a node type without reporting them. For example `pre_actions` on a `conversation` node is dropped. Read a created workflow back if you are unsure what was stored.
88	
89	### Update a workflow
90	
91	`PUT /api/v2/workflow/{workflowId}`
92	
93	```bash
94	curl -s -X PUT "$FREYA_API_URL/api/v2/workflow/$WORKFLOW_ID" \
95	  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FREYA_API_KEY" \
96	  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
97	  -H "User-Agent: $UA" \
98	  -d '{"workflow": {"initial_node": "start", "nodes": {}, "global_nodes": {}}}'
99	```
100	
101	The body replaces the whole definition. A top-level key that your new definition leaves out is deleted, including `test_variables` and an `agent_config` that the platform filled in. Send the complete definition every time.
102	
103	An update saves a new version and does NOT publish it. Simulations and calls run the published version, so after an update alone you are still testing the old phone agent. Publish the new version:
104	
105	```bash
106	# newest version first
107	curl -s "$FREYA_API_URL/api/v2/versions/workflow/$WORKFLOW_ID?workspaceId=$WORKSPACE_ID" -H "Authorization: Bearer $FREYA_API_KEY" -H "User-Agent: $UA"
108	# result.versions[] has id, versionNumber, isPublished
109	
110	curl -s -X POST "$FREYA_API_URL/api/v2/versions/workflow/$WORKFLOW_ID/publish" \
111	  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FREYA_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "User-Agent: $UA" \
112	  -d '{"versionId": "<id of the newest version>"}'
113	```
114	
115	`freya.update_workflow` and `freya.save_workflow` do both steps. A run of a simulation reports the version it used as `agentVersionNumber`. Check it when a change seems to have no effect.
116	
117	### Get a workflow
118	
119	`GET /api/v2/workflow/{workflowId}`
120	
121	```bash
122	curl -s "$FREYA_API_URL/api/v2/workflow/$WORKFLOW_ID" \
123	  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FREYA_API_KEY" \
124	  -H "User-Agent: $UA"
125	```
126	
127	The path is the same as for update. The reference client does not call this route, so the fields of its result are not confirmed.
128	
129	## Workspace
130	
131	`GET /api/v2/workspaces` lists the workspaces your key can see. The list is at `result.workspaces`. Each entry has an `id`.
132	
133	```bash
134	curl -s "$FREYA_API_URL/api/v2/workspaces" \
135	  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FREYA_API_KEY" \
136	  -H "User-Agent: $UA"
137	```
138	
139	List routes need the workspace id as a query parameter. The name of that parameter is not confirmed here. See https://docs.freyavoice.ai.
140	
141	## Personas
142	
143	A persona plays the caller in a simulation. It has a prompt and success criteria.
144	
145	### Create personas
146	
147	`POST /api/v2/personas`
148	
149	```bash
150	curl -s -X POST "$FREYA_API_URL/api/v2/personas" \
151	  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FREYA_API_KEY" \
152	  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
153	  -H "User-Agent: $UA" \
154	  -d '{"personas": [{"name": "Late parcel", "prompt": "You are Dana Reed. Your parcel is five days late. Answer what you are asked in one short sentence.", "successCriteria": "The agent states the new delivery day.", "tags": ["practice"]}]}'
155	```
156	
157	| Field | Meaning |
158	|---|---|
159	| `personas[].name` | Persona name |
160	| `personas[].prompt` | Instructions for the model that plays the caller |
161	| `personas[].successCriteria` | Text that the judge model checks after the call |
162	| `personas[].tags` | Array of strings |
163	
164	The created personas are at `result.personas`, in request order. Each has an `id`.
165	
166	### List personas
167	
168	`GET /api/v2/personas`
169	
170	```bash
171	curl -s "$FREYA_API_URL/api/v2/personas" \
172	  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FREYA_API_KEY" \
173	  -H "User-Agent: $UA"
174	```
175	
176	Not confirmed: the reference client only creates personas. The path above is the create route with `GET`. This is a list route, so it needs the workspace query parameter mentioned above. Take the parameters and result fields from https://docs.freyavoice.ai.
177	
178	## Simulations
179	
180	A simulation runs your agent against personas. In `chat` mode the conversation is text only.
181	
182	### Create a simulation
183	
184	`POST /api/v2/simulations`
185	
186	```bash
187	curl -s -X POST "$FREYA_API_URL/api/v2/simulations" \
188	  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FREYA_API_KEY" \
189	  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
190	  -H "User-Agent: $UA" \
191	  -d '{
192	    "agentId": "AGENT_ID",
193	    "name": "practice run 1",
194	    "mode": "chat",
195	    "selectedPersonaIds": ["PERSONA_ID"],
196	    "customerVariablesMap": {"PERSONA_ID": {"customer_id": "c_123", "first_name": "Dana"}},
197	    "maxConcurrentCalls": 5,
198	    "runsPerPersona": 1,
199	    "maxCallDurationSeconds": 420,
200	    "assistantLlmOverride": {"provider": "experimental-5", "model": "experimental-5"},
201	    "routingLlmOverride": {"provider": "experimental-5", "model": "experimental-5"},
202	    "extractionLlmOverride": {"provider": "experimental-5", "model": "experimental-5"},
203	    "personaLlmOverride": {"provider": "google", "model": "gemini-3-flash-preview"},
204	    "analysisLlmOverride": {"provider": "google", "model": "gemini-3-flash-preview"}
205	  }'
206	```
207	
208	| Field | Meaning |
209	|---|---|
210	| `agentId` | `workflow.agentId` from the create call |
211	| `name` | Name of the simulation |
212	| `mode` | `"chat"` for a text simulation |
213	| `selectedPersonaIds` | Persona ids to run |
214	| `customerVariablesMap` | Object keyed by persona id. Each value is the object of call variables for that persona's call |
215	| `maxConcurrentCalls` | How many calls run at the same time |
216	| `runsPerPersona` | Calls per persona |
217	| `maxCallDurationSeconds` | Limit for one call |
218	| `assistantLlmOverride` | Model for the dialogue call. Object with `provider` and `model` |
219	| `routingLlmOverride` | Model for the routing call |
220	| `extractionLlmOverride` | Model for the extraction call |
221	| `personaLlmOverride` | Model that plays the caller |
222	| `analysisLlmOverride` | Model that judges the success criteria |
223	
224	Pass all three agent overrides (`assistantLlmOverride`, `routingLlmOverride`, `extractionLlmOverride`) on every simulation. An override you leave out falls back to the agent's default model. The values above are the ones the reference client uses. Use the models your event rules name.
225	
226	The simulation id is at `result.simulation.id`.
227	
228	### Poll a simulation
229	
230	`GET /api/v2/simulations/{simulationId}`
231	
232	```bash
233	curl -s "$FREYA_API_URL/api/v2/simulations/$SIM_ID" \
234	  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FREYA_API_KEY" \
235	  -H "User-Agent: $UA"
236	```
237	
238	Read `result.simulation.status`. Poll every 10 seconds until it is `completed`, `failed` or `paused`. Other status values are not listed in the sources.
239	
240	### Talk to your workflow turn by turn
241	
242	`POST /api/v2/chat/message` runs one turn against the published workflow, with no simulation and no queue. It answers in seconds, so it is the fastest way to see whether a workflow starts at all and what it says first.
243	
244	```bash
245	curl -s -X POST "$FREYA_API_URL/api/v2/chat/message" \
246	  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FREYA_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "User-Agent: $UA" \
247	  -d '{"workflowId": "'$WORKFLOW_ID'", "message": "Hello?", "customerVariables": {"customer_id": "c_test", "first_name": "Daniel", "last_name": "Reyes", "title": "Mr", "now": "2026-10-14T11:00"}}'
248	```
249	
250	`result` has `response` (what the phone agent said) and `callId`. Send the next turn with the same `callId`. End it with `POST /api/v2/chat/end` and `{"callId": "..."}`.
251	
252	Seen in tests, not guaranteed: a long turn can return 504, and when the first step is a code step the chat route may skip it, so values that step computes are empty. A bare 500 here means the workflow cannot start a call at all.
253	
254	### List iterations
255	
256	`GET /api/v2/simulations/{simulationId}/iterations`
257	
258	```bash
259	curl -s "$FREYA_API_URL/api/v2/simulations/$SIM_ID/iterations" \
260	  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FREYA_API_KEY" \
261	  -H "User-Agent: $UA"
262	```
263	
264	An iteration is one execution of the simulation. The list is at `result.iterations`. The reference client takes the first entry's `id` right after a simulation finishes.
265	
266	### Get an iteration's runs
267	
268	`GET /api/v2/simulations/{simulationId}/iterations/{iterationId}`
269	
270	```bash
271	curl -s "$FREYA_API_URL/api/v2/simulations/$SIM_ID/iterations/$ITERATION_ID" \
272	  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FREYA_API_KEY" \
273	  -H "User-Agent: $UA"
274	```
275	
276	`result` has `iteration`, `runs` and `runsTotal`. A run is one call with one persona.
277	
278	| Field of a run | Meaning |
279	|---|---|
280	| `id` | Run id |
281	| `callId` | Id of the call. Use it to fetch the transcript |
282	| `personaId`, `personaName` | The persona that played the caller |
283	| `outcome` | Result of the success criteria, for example `fail` |
284	| `reason` | The judge's explanation |
285	| `turnCount` | Number of turns |
286	| `startedAt`, `endedAt` | Timestamps |
287	
288	The route returns 30 runs unless you ask for more. Pass `limit` (100 at most) and `offset`, and read until a page comes back short. Compare the number you read with `runsTotal`. `freya.get_iteration` does this for you.
289	
290	While a simulation is running, `outcome` is `queued` or `running` for the runs that have not finished.
291	
292	## Calls
293	
294	### Get a call with its transcript
295	
296	`GET /api/v2/call/{callId}`
297	
298	```bash
299	curl -s "$FREYA_API_URL/api/v2/call/$CALL_ID" \
300	  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FREYA_API_KEY" \
301	  -H "User-Agent: $UA"
302	```
303	
304	The call is at `result.call`.
305	
306	| Field | Meaning |
307	|---|---|
308	| `messages` | The event list of the call. See below |
309	| `transcript` | The conversation as one text string |
310	| `endedReason` | Why the call ended. For an `end_call` node it is the terminal's `function.name` |
311	| `duration` | Seconds |
312	| `successCriteriaResult` | Object with `success` and `reason` |
313	
314	Each entry of `messages` has `role`, `message`, `nodeId`, `messageId` and `secondsFromStart`.
315	
316	| `role` | `message` contains |
317	|---|---|
318	| `assistant` | What the agent said |
319	| `user` | What the caller said |
320	| `system` | A JSON string that describes one engine event |
321	
322	System events seen in a trial call:
323	
324	| `event` | Content |
325	|---|---|
326	| `node_enter` | `node`, `from_node`, `reason` |
327	| `function_call_start` | `function` and `args`. For an `api_call` the args are the full request: `url`, `method`, `headers`, `body` |
328	| `function_call_complete` | `function` and `result` |
329	| `route_evaluated` | `matched`, `from_node`, `target`, `reason`, a `branches` list with the result of every condition, and `variable_table` with all variables at that moment |
330	| `error` | `message` and `details` |
331	
332	`route_evaluated` is the fastest way to learn why a transition did or did not fire. Each branch shows the variable, the operand and the result.
333	
334	User and assistant messages in the trial call also carried a `workflowSnapshot` with `currentNode`, `previousNode`, `nodeTurnCount`, `totalTurnCount`, `transitionHistory`, `enteredNodes` and `variableTable`. Each entry of `variableTable` has `value`, `confidence`, `source` and `source_node`. Whether a query parameter is needed to receive the snapshots is not confirmed.
335	
336	To check whether a variable arrived, read `variable_table` or `variableTable`. Finding the variable's name in a prompt or in a code body proves nothing about its value.
337	
338	## A minimal loop
339	
340	1. Build the workflow JSON.
341	2. `POST /api/v2/workflow?dryRun=true` and fix what it rejects.
342	3. `POST /api/v2/workflow`. Keep `workflow.agentId`.
343	4. `POST /api/v2/personas` once. Keep the ids.
344	5. `POST /api/v2/simulations` with the agent id, the persona ids and the call variables.
345	6. Poll `GET /api/v2/simulations/{id}` until the status is final.
346	7. `GET .../iterations`, then `GET .../iterations/{id}` for the runs.
347	8. For each failed run, `GET /api/v2/call/{callId}` and read the events.
348	
349	For everything else, see https://docs.freyavoice.ai.
350
